SAN JOSE, Calif., October 15, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Super Micro Computer, Inc. (Nasdaq: SMCI), an AI, Enterprise, Storage, and 5G/Edge Total IT Solution Provider featuring Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), today announced the appointment of Mark Long as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer reporting directly to the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Charles Liang, effective immediately.

Mr. Long is a seasoned finance executive with decades of experience across the technology sector spanning corporate finance, strategy, mergers and acquisitions, and capital allocation. He previously served as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of Western Digital, where he led financial management, investor relations and corporate strategy, and played a central role in building a scaled, global data infrastructure leader. Mr. Long previously served as co-founder and Partner of Prime Impact Capital, a technology-focused investment firm, was a Senior Vice President of Strategy and Corporate Development at Hitachi Global Storage Technologies and, earlier in his career, held senior roles in investment banking focused on the software, cloud infrastructure, and storage sectors.

"We are pleased to welcome Mark to the Supermicro executive team and look forward to benefitting from his deep strategic expertise and proven leadership," said Charles Liang, Founder, President, and CEO of Supermicro. "I'm confident Mark will have an immediate positive impact in strengthening and accelerating our operational and financial execution as we continue to scale our business to capture the next wave of AI and IT infrastructure growth."

Liang continued, "We are also grateful to David Weigand for his many years of service as CFO and for his support of an orderly transition."

"I am honored to join Supermicro as it continues to build on its leadership in AI and high-performance infrastructure," said Mr. Long. "Charles has built a remarkable company, and I look forward to partnering closely with him and the executive team to scale the business effectively and efficiently – strengthening our financial foundation while supporting continued innovation, growth, and long-term value creation for shareholders."

The company conducted an extensive search process to identify and secure an exceptional candidate with the necessary skills and experience. Mr. Long succeeds David Weigand. David will assist in the transition and shift his focus to helping optimize and accelerate the business.

title: Is SMCI Stock A Real Bargain?
detail:
Is SMCI Stock A Real Bargain?
Trefis Team
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 5:52 AM PDT 3 min read
SMCI
DELL
HPE
ANET
CSCO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shares of Super Micro Computer (SMCI) trade at 9.8 times earnings. The median S&P 500 company trades at 22.7. Over the past year, Super Micro stock lost 34.6%, while the broader index returned 17.3%. This low price could point to a fast-growing server maker on sale, or it might reflect a fair price for profits that may not turn into cash. So does Super Micro's profit back up the low price?

Super Micro's Profit Has More Than Doubled

The company earned $2.23 billion in the twelve months to June 2026, compared with $1.05 billion a year earlier. Revenue grew 77.8% over those twelve months, while the median S&P 500 company grew 8.3%. Super Micro sells mainly servers: server and storage systems made up 97% of its revenue in fiscal 2025, the twelve months to June 2025.

Super Micro has maintained its operating margin during this rapid expansion. Operating margin was 7.1% over the twelve months to June 2026, roughly in line with its 7.0% average over the three latest twelve-month periods. Gross margin was 10.8% over the same twelve months, below its 11.9% average. The low P/E is not a discount on shrinking profit.

Did Super Micro's Operations Bring In Money?

No. Over the same twelve months, Super Micro's operations used $6.81 billion of cash. A year earlier, they brought in $1.66 billion. A single quarter accounted for most of the outflow, with operations using $6.62 billion from January to March 2026.

Super Micro has used cash during periods of rapid growth before. In the twelve months to June 2024, when revenue more than doubled, its operations used $2.49 billion of cash. In two of the last three years, Super Micro reported a profit while its operations paid out more cash than they took in.

Inflow Returned From April To June, But Debt Grew

After three quarters in which they used cash, Super Micro's operations brought in $747 million of cash from April to June 2026. This inflow remained below the $864 million recorded in the same quarter a year earlier. Sales from April to June 2026 nearly doubled from a year earlier, and cash came in alongside the growth. Each dollar of sales also kept more profit: gross margin was 17.5% that quarter, compared with 9.5% in the same quarter a year earlier.

The company also carries more debt than it did a year ago. Total debt was $8.76 billion at June 30, 2026, up from $4.78 billion a year earlier. On the same date, it held $7.52 billion of cash and short-term investments. A P/E counts only earnings, leaving out both the debt and the cash.

Super Micro is growing its profit, but whether that profit arrives as cash remains an open question after one good quarter. A buyer at this price is betting that Super Micro can keep its operations bringing in cash, not that the market has misjudged a healthy business. The crucial metric to watch is cash from operations for the July to September 2026 quarter, detailed in the report expected on or around November 3, 2026. Seeing cash come in again would support the bet, while a return to using cash would undercut it.

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after a broad pickup in energy expenses lifted September inflation to 3.7%, surpassing expectations and driving bond yields higher.

The hotter-than-anticipated inflation reading dampened market sentiment across Wall Street, weighing heavily on major benchmark indexes and pulling equities down from recent highs. When inflation accelerates, it often increases expectations that borrowing costs will remain elevated for an extended period to curb economic overheating. Elevated interest rates can compress corporate valuations, particularly across growth sectors such as technology and semiconductors, where future earnings expectations play a central role in pricing.

Semiconductor shares faced extended pressure, marking their seventh consecutive session of declines as market participants recalibrated risk appetites. Beyond higher financing expenses, persistent energy-driven inflation risks squeezing operating margins and weakening broader enterprise spending. Digi Power X pairs owned power infrastructure with Supermicro GPUs to serve enterprise AI customers Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Digi Power X Inc (NASDAQ:DGXX, FRA:1NQ0, NEO:DGX) is using Super Micro Computer Inc (NASDAQ:SMCI) servers built around Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips to sell AI computing capacity to enterprise customers, according to a Supermicro case study.

The company owns and operates the infrastructure behind its NeoCloudz platform, from power generation and substations to Tier III data centers. NeoCloudz rents GPU capacity on dedicated bare-metal servers, with no virtualization layer and no sharing of hardware among customers. The servers can be hosted at a Digi Power X facility or installed at a customer's site.

Digi Power X deployed Supermicro systems with Nvidia B200 and B300 GPUs, liquid cooling and Supermicro management software, the case study highlighted.

Supermicro said it wanted hardware that could handle both large-scale AI training and real-time inference.

The company said its ownership of power assets, including substations and on-site generation, sets it apart from traditional cloud providers. It said GPU rental rates reflect its actual power costs rather than the margins charged by those providers. It also said liquid-cooled, high-density racks fit more computing into less floor space, which lowers the cost per GPU-hour passed on to customers. As a result, Digi Power X said, it can offer Blackwell compute at rates traditional providers can't match.

Scalability was another priority. Digi Power X said it aims to add capacity in weeks rather than years, without large upfront capital outlays at each stage of growth.

For orchestration and billing, the company integrated three Supermicro software products: SuperCloud Composer, SuperCloud Developer Experience and SuperCloud Director. They give customers visibility into their workloads and automated, metered billing.

The data center environment includes high-density GPU rack rows with per-cabinet power monitoring, hot-aisle containment, expansion-ready room layouts and rack-level environmental sensing.

"DigiPowerX was built on the conviction that the AI infrastructure market needed a fundamentally different model — one where the operator controls the full stack, from power to compute, and passes those structural advantages directly to customers," said Alec Amar, president of Digi Power X.

"Supermicro has been a critical partner in executing that vision, giving us access to the latest NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and the software tooling to manage it at scale. The result is a platform we are proud to be already running in production for enterprise AI customers today."

The platform is already running in production for enterprise customers, the case study said.

title: What Was HPE Telling You Before Its Stock Ran?
detail:
What Was HPE Telling You Before Its Stock Ran?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) stock returned 187.1%, counting dividends, in the twelve months to October 13, 2026. On September 2, 2026, the company reported record quarterly revenue, orders, and backlog. Executives credited demand for traditional servers, AI systems and networking, along with higher prices for those servers. Did the company say anything about that demand, or those server prices, before October 2025?

HPE Praised AI Demand, Then Faulted Its Own Pricing

Executives addressed these trends twice, though only one instance sounded like good news at the time. During the December 5, 2024 call for fiscal Q4 2024, management noted that demand for AI systems remained strong. Revenue for that quarter reached a record $8.5 billion, up 15.1% from a year earlier.

Three months later, during the March 6, 2025 call for fiscal Q1 2025, executives identified servers as a problem. Management stated that HPE had priced its traditional servers without fully accounting for the value of its inventory, and that unusually high AI inventory had squeezed server margins further. Server operating margin stood at 8.1%, a figure management called well below expectations. The shares struggled after that report. Only in hindsight does this look like a sign, because server pricing is exactly what management would highlight eighteen months later.

Financial filings from HPE showed this same mix of rising sales and weaker margins. Revenue grew 18.5% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2025. Yet operating margin for that quarter fell to 4.7%, down from 7.8% a year earlier. The stock was already rising as well: it returned 74.7% in the six months before the twelve-month window began on October 10, 2025.

How Big Was HPE's Run Against The S&P 500?

The S&P 500 returned about 18% over the same twelve months. That means HPE returned roughly ten times as much as the broader index. Almost all of that gain materialized in the last six months, when the stock returned 183%. HPE was not alone in this trend: Dell Technologies, one of its peers, did even better at 285.0%. Not every peer joined in, though, as IBM fell 14.8%.

The shift linking back to those earlier earnings calls occurred in servers, HPE's largest business at 52% of fiscal 2025 revenue. Server revenue rose 35% to an all-time high in fiscal Q3 2026. Executives noted that higher average selling prices for traditional servers made up for supply limits on how many units HPE could ship. This trajectory looks like the March 2025 pricing problem reversed.
